extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent applicants/practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining inherency, anticipation, and obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §102 and §103 for compositions, products, apparatus, processes, and product-by-process claims; explains burdens of proof and required examiner reasoning. Includes cases and examples illustrating when prior art's implicit or inherent properties defeat patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Something which is old does not become patentable upon the discovery of a new property
rubrics_metrics.description: "[T]he discovery of a previously unappreciated property of a prior art composition, or of a scientific explanation for the prior art’s functioning, does not render the old composition patentably new to the discoverer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming a new use, new function or unknown property which is inherently present in the prior art does not necessarily make the claim patentable. Cited cases: Atlas Powder Co. v. IRECO Inc., In re Best, In re Crish (example where sequencing a known plasmid did not render claimed oligonucleotides novel). See MPEP § 2112.01 for related identification guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent feature need not be recognized at the time of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no requirement that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized the inherent disclosure at the time of invention; only that the subject matter is in fact inherent in the prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A characteristic that is a necessary feature or result of a prior-art embodiment is enough for inherent anticipation even if unknown at the time. Cited cases: Schering Corp. v. Geneva Pharm., Toro Co. v. Deere & Co., Abbott Labs v. Geneva Pharms., Atlas Powder Co. v. IRECO, SmithKline Beecham Corp. v. Apotex, In re Omeprazole (examples showing inherent properties need not be recognized contemporaneously).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 can be made when prior art product appears identical but is silent as to an inherent characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Where applicant claims a composition in terms of a function, property or characteristic and the composition of the prior art is the same as that of the claim but the function is not explicitly disclosed, the examiner may make a rejection under both 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is nothing inconsistent in concurrent rejections for obviousness and anticipation. This rationale applies to product, apparatus, and process claims recited in terms of function/property/characteristic. Cited case: In re Best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must provide rationale or evidence to show inherency
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that a certain result or characteristic may occur or be present in the prior art is not sufficient to establish inherency; the examiner must provide objective evidence or cogent technical reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In relying upon inherency, the examiner must provide a basis in fact and/or technical reasoning to reasonably support the determination that the characteristic necessarily flows from the teachings of the applied prior art. Mere invitation to investigate or optimization-based inferences are insufficient. Cited authorities and examples: Ex parte Levy (basis in fact/technical reasoning required), In re Rijckaert (rejection reversed where inherency based on optimization), In re Oelrich, Metabolite Labs. (genus vs species), and the Schreiber example (where Board reversed for lack of evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shifts to applicant after examiner establishes inherency for substantially identical prior-art product
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a reference teaching a product appearing to be substantially identical is made the basis of a rejection, and the examiner presents evidence or reasoning to show inherency, the burden of production shifts to the applicant to show the prior art does not possess the characteristics relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO can require applicant to prove that prior art products do not necessarily or inherently possess the claimed characteristics; burden similar to product-by-process contexts. Cited cases/examples: In re Best, In re Fitzgerald (applicant needed objective evidence comparing shrinkage rates), Schreiber (applicant declaration failed because it lacked necessary specifics). See MPEP § 2113 for product-by-process discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product and apparatus claims: substantially identical structure/composition presumes claimed properties/functions are inherent
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claimed and prior art products are identical or substantially identical in structure or composition, or are produced by identical or substantially identical processes, a prima facie case of either anticipation or obviousness has been established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the PTO shows a sound basis for believing products are the same, applicant has the burden of showing they are not. Cases: In re Best, Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner, In re Ludtke, Northam Warren Corp. v. D. F. Newfield. Examiner should rely on evidence of substantial identity; applicant can rebut with evidence showing prior art products do not necessarily possess the characteristics of the claimed product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition claims: identical chemical structure implies identical properties
rubrics_metrics.description: "Products of identical chemical composition can not have mutually exclusive properties." If the prior art teaches the identical chemical structure, the properties applicant discloses/claims are necessarily present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtual identity of monomers and procedures can support a prima facie case of lack of novelty (In re Spada). Applicant must provide evidence of nonobvious or distinguishing properties to rebut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter that is nonfunctional does not distinguish a claimed product from otherwise identical prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the only difference between a prior art product and a claimed product is printed matter that is not functionally related to the product, the printed matter will not distinguish the claimed product from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical question: whether there exists a new and unobvious functional relationship between the printed matter and the substrate. Cases/examples: In re Ngai (kit with different instructions still anticipated), In re Gulack, In re Miller (writing showing how to 'half' a recipe was functional), In re Seid, In re Xiao, In re Bryan. Extension: instruction limitations added to known methods are treated similarly (King Pharmaceuticals v. Eon Labs; In re Kao).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims: prior art device anticipates a claimed process if device would necessarily perform the method during normal operation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art device, in its normal and usual operation, would necessarily perform the method claimed, then the method claimed will be considered anticipated by the prior art device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the prior art device is the same as a device described in the specification for carrying out the claimed method, it can be assumed the device will inherently perform the claimed process. Examples/cases: In re King (coated substrate inherently performs claimed absorption/reflection process), In re Best (cooling step inherently performed), Ex parte Novitski, Ex parte Novitski and others where applicants failed to introduce comparative evidence to rebut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-of-use claims: new and nonobvious uses of old structures/compositions may be patentable, but claims directed to a result/property may be anticipated
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of a new use for an old structure based on unknown properties might be patentable as a process of using; however, when the claim recites using an old composition or structure and the 'use' is directed to a result or property of that composition/structure, then the claim is anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re Hack (new use possibly patentable), In re May (claims to a method of achieving nonaddictive analgesia were anticipated because prior art taught same compounds for analgesia), In re Tomlinson (result of mixing was not enough to avoid anticipation). Applicants must show unexpected properties or nonobviousness to prevail on use claims directed to properties/results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims: product patentability is based on the product itself, not the recited process
rubrics_metrics.description: "Even though product-by-process claims are limited by and defined by the process, determination of patentability is based on the product itself. If the product in the product-by-process claim is the same as or obvious from a product of the prior art, the claim is unpatentable even though the prior product was made by a different process."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product identity or obviousness from prior art products defeats product-by-process claims even if made by different processes (In re Thorpe, Amgen v. F. Hoffmann-La Roche, Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma). However, in infringement analysis, a product-by-process claim is infringed only by a product made by the recited process. Consider the structure implied by the process steps when assessing patentability (In re Garnero, In re Nordt Dev. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shifts to applicant for product-by-process claims once examiner shows claimed product appears identical
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office bears a lesser burden in making out a prima facie case of obviousness for product-by-process claims; once examiner provides a rationale tending to show the claimed product appears the same as the prior art product produced by a different process, the burden shifts to applicant to present evidence of a nonobvious difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re Fessmann, In re Marosi. Applicant should produce evidence establishing unexpected properties or concrete differences (Ex parte Gray example where comparisons were lacking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection alternatively on 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 for product-by-process claims is acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior art discloses a product which reasonably appears to be identical with or only slightly different than a product claimed in a product-by-process claim, a rejection based alternatively on section 102 or section 103 is fair and acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office may rely on alternative grounds of anticipation or obviousness for product-by-process claims, but must explain both the anticipation and obviousness aspects of the rejections. Cited case: In re Brown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency and functional limitations in apparatus claims: examiner must explain inherency of functional limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner concludes that a functional limitation is an inherent characteristic of the prior art, the examiner should explain that the prior art structure inherently possesses the functionally defined limitations of the claimed apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inherency of function is asserted, burden shifts to applicant to establish that the prior art does not possess the characteristic relied on. Cases: In re Schreiber (examiner justified in concluding inherent function based on structural similarity), Bettcher Industries v. Bunzl USA, In re Swinehart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of operating a device does not differentiate an apparatus claim from the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A]pparatus claims cover what a device is, not what a device does." A recitation of the manner in which an apparatus is intended to be employed does not differentiate the claimed apparatus if the prior art teaches all structural limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational or use-oriented preambles are immaterial to the structure; Ex parte Masham example (submersion amount immaterial). Case: Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Bausch & Lomb Inc.

rubrics_metrics.name: A prior art device can perform all functions recited in an apparatus claim and still not anticipate if there is any structural difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the prior art device performs all claimed functions, the prior art cannot anticipate the claim if there is any structural difference required by the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means-plus-function limitations are met by structures equivalent to those in the specification. Cases: In re Donaldson, In re Robertson (claim construed to require three fastening elements; reference with two elements did not disclose a separate third element). Examiner should analyze structural elements, not solely functional equivalence.
